What does 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17 teach about being "caught up"?
It teaches the resurrection of the dead in Christ and the change of living believers to meet the Lord. It says nothing of a tribulation, seven years, or a return to heaven.

Paul comforts grieving believers. The dead in Christ will rise first. Then believers who are alive will be "caught up" with them to meet the Lord, and so they will always be with him. The Latin Bible rendered "caught up" as rapiemur, from which the word "rapture" comes. Most amillennial and postmillennial readers see this as the general resurrection at Christ's final coming. As Anthony Hoekema noted, the passage does not say the Lord then turns back to heaven for seven years. The Greek word for "meet" (apantēsis) was used for citizens going out to welcome a visiting ruler and escort him back to their city (Acts 28:15). On that reading, believers meet Christ and come with him, not leave with him.
Acts 28:15: believers from Rome came out to meet Paul at the Forum of Appius and then went back with him to the city. The same word for "meeting" is used.
Matthew 25:6: the virgins go out "to meet" the bridegroom and then enter the feast with him.

Pre-tribulation teachers read the passage as the rapture itself. They point to its comfort, its focus on the church, and its lack of signs. Some full preterists see the coming as already past in AD 70. Partial preterists, like most Christians, place this resurrection still in the future.
How old is the teaching of a pre-tribulation rapture?
As a clear system it appears around 1830, with John Nelson Darby and the Plymouth Brethren. Earlier claimed hints, such as Pseudo-Ephraem and Morgan Edwards, are disputed.

The church's creeds and main teachers from the second century to the nineteenth expected one future coming of Christ, with the resurrection and judgment together. A pre-tribulation dispensationalist, H. A. Ironside, admitted in 1908 that the teaching is scarcely found in any book or sermon over 1600 years. As a system it grew with J. N. Darby and the Brethren in the 1830s. Some writers link it to a vision of Margaret MacDonald in 1830, though that link is debated. Others point to Morgan Edwards (a Baptist student essay of 1744, printed 1788). Supporters also cite a sermon by "Pseudo-Ephraem". Its date is uncertain (suggested from the fourth to the seventh century), and its meaning is disputed. The fulfilled reading argues that a key doctrine should not depend on such thin witnesses.
1830: Margaret MacDonald's vision in Port Glasgow, Scotland, later cited in debates about the teaching's origin.
1788: Morgan Edwards's essay, printed in Philadelphia, which some say places the saints' removal before part of the end-time events.

Pre-tribulation scholars reply that age does not decide truth. The Reformation itself recovered neglected truths. They also argue that early writers held to imminence, which they see as the seed of the doctrine. They read Pseudo-Ephraem as a real early witness to a rescue before the tribulation.
If the timing of the rapture is a "deduction" from a system, what does that mean for the doctrine?
On the fulfilled reading, it means the system came first and texts were then fitted to it. A central doctrine should rest on clear Scripture, not only inference.

One leading defender of the pre-tribulation view wrote that neither side has a proof text for timing, so the question is decided by deduction from one's whole theology. He named Revelation 3:10 as a possible exception. The fulfilled reading sees a problem of method here. A system is built first, then doctrines are made to keep it working, and then a teaching unknown for centuries is called biblical. Paul praised hearers who checked his words against Scripture (Acts 17:11). Christians do use inference for some doctrines, but a doctrine that shapes how millions see the future should show clear textual roots. This reading argues that the rapture timing does not.
Compare the Trinity: it is drawn from many plain statements (Matthew 28:19; John 1:1; 2 Corinthians 13:14). Pre-tribulation timing lacks any statement of the gap it needs.

Pre-tribulation defenders say all views of timing use inference, including post-tribulation views. They hold that their deduction is the best fit for imminence, the promise of escape from wrath and the Israel-church distinction. They add that some of their writers have since argued that Revelation 3:10 gives direct support.
What is the "hour of testing" in Revelation 3:10?
On the fulfilled reading, it is the trial "about to come" on the Roman world in John's day, ending in Jerusalem's fall. The promise was made to the church in Philadelphia.

Jesus tells the church in Philadelphia: because you kept my word, I will keep you from the hour of testing that is about to come on the whole inhabited world (oikoumenē). The Greek word mellō ("about to") points to something near. Oikoumenē often means the Roman world (Luke 2:1). The promise was given to a real congregation, which would gain nothing from a rescue twenty centuries later. On this reading the "hour" is the time of upheaval from about AD 64 to 70: Nero's persecution, the Jewish war and the civil wars of AD 68-69. Christians in Judea escaped by fleeing as Jesus warned (Matthew 24:16). "Keep from" (tēreō ek) is the same phrase Jesus used in John 17:15, where he asks that the disciples be kept from evil while staying in the world.
Luke 2:1: Augustus taxed "all the world" (oikoumenē), which means the Roman Empire.
Eusebius (Church History 3.5.3) reports that Jerusalem's Christians left for Pella before the war's end.

Pre-tribulation scholars argue that "keep from the hour" means removal from the very time of trial, not protection within it. They take "the whole world" and "those who dwell on the earth" as the global end-time tribulation. Post-tribulation scholars agree with the fulfilled reading that tēreō ek can mean protection in the trial, though they place the trial in the future.
Is the "blessed hope" in Titus 2:13 a different event from the appearing of Christ's glory?
No. Grammatically the blessed hope and the appearing are one event. Even John Walvoord agreed that Titus 2:13 describes a single event.

Paul says believers wait for "the blessed hope and appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ". In Greek, one article governs both nouns ("hope" and "appearing"), which joins them as one thing seen two ways. Dave Hunt read the blessed hope as the rapture and the appearing as a later coming seven years on. The text does not separate them. On the fulfilled reading, the verse also stresses the appearing of "the glory", which links it to Jesus' promise that the Son of Man would come in his Father's glory within the lifetime of some who stood there (Matthew 16:27-28). Paul and Titus expected that unveiling of Christ's glory to touch their own day.
The same grammar joins "God and Savior" into one Person in this verse; the same rule joins "hope and appearing".
Matthew 16:28: "some standing here ... will in no way taste of death, until they see the Son of Man coming in his Kingdom" (WEB).

Most Christians, including most futurists, agree that Titus 2:13 names one event. They see that event as the future bodily return of Christ at the end of history. Some pre-tribulation teachers still call the rapture the "blessed hope" in a general sense.
On the fulfilled reading, what is the "appearing of the glory" that believers awaited?
It is the full unveiling of the new covenant's glory when the fading old covenant order of temple and sacrifice was removed in AD 70.

Paul contrasts two covenants. The ministry of Moses came with a glory that was fading. The ministry of the Spirit and righteousness has a far greater glory that remains (2 Corinthians 3:7-11). The fulfilled reading holds that the old order, already made obsolete by the cross, was "ready to vanish away" when Hebrews was written (Hebrews 8:13). It ended visibly when the temple, priesthood and sacrifices were destroyed in AD 70. The "appearing of the glory" in Titus 2:13 is then the public display of Christ's glory in vindicating his new covenant people. The gospel is the light of "the glory of Christ" that unbelief cannot see (2 Corinthians 4:3-4). This reading does not deny a future bodily return; it reads this text as near-term.
Hebrews 8:13: the old covenant is "growing aged" and "near to vanishing away" (WEB), written before AD 70.
AD 70: the temple burned in the month of Ab (Josephus, Jewish War 6.4.5-8), and daily sacrifice had already ceased (6.2.1).

Most interpreters, including most amillennial and postmillennial scholars, read the "appearing" (epiphaneia) in the Pastoral Letters as Christ's future personal return (compare 2 Timothy 4:1, 8). They grant the covenant contrast in 2 Corinthians 3 but do not tie Titus 2:13 to AD 70.
What was the "end of all things" that Peter said was "at hand"?
On the fulfilled reading, it was the end of the old covenant order in AD 70, a few years after Peter wrote to Christians already in a "fiery trial".

Peter writes that "the end of all things is at hand" (1 Peter 4:7). His readers were already in a fiery trial (4:12). They would rejoice "at the revelation of his glory" (4:13), and the Spirit of glory already rested on them (4:14). Jay Adams, a Reformed commentator, argued that the letter was written before AD 70, and that the end in view was the overthrow of Jerusalem and its temple system some six or seven years later. The fulfilled reading asks how a revelation of glory twenty centuries later would comfort people suffering then. Paul also speaks of a glory "about to be revealed" (Romans 8:18, mellousan). The time words point to near events.
1 Peter 4:12-13: a fiery trial "among you" now, with joy promised "at the revelation of his glory".
Romans 8:18 in Young's Literal Translation: "the glory about to be revealed in us".

Many futurists and amillennial readers take "at hand" as a statement that the last age has begun, so that the end could come at any time, as in 2 Peter 3:8-9. They read the revelation of glory as the final return of Christ.
Does 1 Corinthians 15:23-24 leave room for a rapture, a later coming and another resurrection after a thousand years?
Not on its plain order: Christ the firstfruits, then those who are Christ's at his coming, then the end. John 5:28-29 places the raising of good and evil in one hour.

Paul gives a sequence: Christ rose first; then those who belong to him rise at his coming; then comes the end, when he hands over the kingdom to the Father after abolishing every rival rule (15:23-24). The chapter speaks of resurrection, not of a secret rapture, a tribulation or an earthly millennium. To fit a pre-tribulation scheme, one must place gaps in these verses: a rapture, a coming seven years later, and the raising of unbelievers a thousand years after that. Jesus said "the hour comes" when all in the tombs will come out, some to life and some to judgment (John 5:28-29). Christ's reign comes before the resurrection, since there must be a kingdom to hand over.
1 Corinthians 15:25-26: he must reign until every enemy is under his feet, and the last enemy is death. The reign runs until the resurrection.
Daniel 12:2 and Acts 24:15 speak of one resurrection of both the just and the unjust.

Premillennial scholars point out that Paul's "then" (eita) can include long gaps, as one already exists between Christ's resurrection and his coming. They read Revelation 20:4-6 as showing a thousand years between the first and second resurrections.
If Revelation mainly described first-century events, does it still speak to Christians today?
Yes. On the fulfilled reading, past fulfilment does not empty a text of meaning, just as the cross and the Exodus are past events that still teach and comfort.

The fulfilled reading holds that Revelation was written before AD 70 to seven real churches, about things that would "shortly" take place (1:1, 3). Some fear this makes the book useless for us. The cross happened before AD 70, but no one says it has no meaning now. Paul says Israel's wilderness history happened as an example and was written for later instruction (1 Corinthians 10:11). In the same way, Revelation shows Christ ruling over empires, judging persecutors, keeping his people and finishing his covenant plan. These truths still guide the church facing pressure and false worship today. The fulfilled reading also warns against letting newspapers lead interpretation. The Bible is the starting point, and God "works all things after the counsel of his will" (Ephesians 1:11).
1 Corinthians 10:11: past events "were written for our admonition".
Psalm 115:3: "our God is in the heavens. He does whatever he pleases" (WEB). This truth guided past and present readers alike.

Idealist readers say Revelation's value lies in timeless symbols of the battle between Christ and evil in every age. Futurists answer that a book mainly about the past would lose its warning for the last generation, and that its central events still lie ahead.
Why can almost any name be made to add up to 666?
Because the counter chooses the alphabet, the language, the spelling and which letters count. With that much freedom, nearly any name can reach 666.

Letters in Hebrew, Greek and Latin also served as numbers, so names could be "counted". But modern schemes change the rules each time. One drops letters that are not Roman numerals. Another starts A at 100. Another adds titles or uses a nickname. A computer program has even been sold that "decodes" phrases, and it gives 666 for New York and Santa Claus. A literary scholar showed the method's weakness with a joke: "cute purple dinosaur" yields 666 by Roman numerals. The fulfilled reading says this is why time texts and context matter. Revelation 13:18 was a riddle for its first readers, with a fixed language and a known person. It was not an open game for every age.
A historian of interpretation counted over a hundred proposed solutions to 666 among British writers from 1560 to 1830 alone.

Many futurists agree that name-counting has been abused. They still expect the number to identify a future ruler clearly when he appears. Some idealists take 666 as a symbol of human failure (six falling short of seven) rather than a name at all.
Can hidden words in modern terms, like "TeLeviSion", reveal Bible prophecy?
No. Breaking English words into pieces of other languages is not interpretation. The same trick can "prove" opposite things.

One prophecy book claimed that "television" hides Te (tellurium, from tellus, earth), Levi and Sion, so it must be Satan's tool to tell his false gospel. The method takes fragments of a modern word and gives them meanings the word never had. "Television" comes from Greek tele (far) and Latin visio (sight); it means seeing at a distance. One can play the same game in reverse: Jesus told his disciples to "tell the vision" to no one until he rose (Matthew 17:9), so television must now be allowed! The joke shows the method has no limits. The meaning of 666 must come from the Bible and its setting, not from word puzzles in a language John never used.
Matthew 17:9: "Don't tell anyone what you saw, until the Son of Man has risen from the dead" (WEB). A play on words could "prove" anything from this.
Deuteronomy 29:29: the secret things belong to God; the revealed things belong to us.

Few scholars of any school defend such wordplay. Some popular futurist writers still see modern media as a likely tool for the beast's worldwide image and worship (Revelation 13:14-15), without relying on hidden words.
Are "Antichrist" and "the beast" the same person in the Bible?
Not necessarily. "Antichrist" is John's word in his letters for those who deny Christ; "the beast" is a figure in Revelation. Popular teaching often merges them.

Many Christians hear "Antichrist" and picture the beast of Revelation 13. Some writers list ten or more titles, from Daniel, Paul and John, as names of one man. Yet the word "antichrist" appears only in 1 John 2:18, 22; 4:3 and 2 John 7. There it means anyone who denies that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh. A "false Christ" (pseudochristos, Matthew 24:24) is someone who claims to be Messiah. That is a different thing again. The beast of Revelation is a ruling power that persecutes the saints. The fulfilled reading treats these as separate biblical ideas, each with its own setting. Merging them creates a figure no single text describes.
1 John 2:22 defines an antichrist as the liar who denies that Jesus is the Christ.
Matthew 24:24 speaks of "false christs" (plural) who perform signs to deceive.

Most futurists, and many historic interpreters, hold that the man of lawlessness, the beast and the final antichrist are one end-time person. They argue that John's "antichrist is coming" (1 John 2:18) shows the church expected one supreme figure beyond the many lesser ones.
Why did many Protestants identify the papacy as the Antichrist?
They read the "temple of God" in 2 Thessalonians 2:4 as the church, saw Rome as a false church, and read "anti" as "in place of" Christ.

From the Reformation until the nineteenth century, many Protestants named the papal office as the man of sin and Rome as the harlot of Revelation 17. The Westminster Confession (1646) called the pope "that Antichrist" (25.6). The reasoning ran like this. Paul's "temple of God" was taken to mean the church, since the church is called God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16-17; Ephesians 2:20-21). A false leader seated in the church fitted the papacy. The Greek prefix anti can mean "against" or "instead of", and the pope's title "Vicar of Christ" seemed to claim Christ's place. The fulfilled reading notes that this view, like modern ones, ignores Revelation's time markers. It also reads Paul's temple outside its first-century setting.
The 1646 Westminster Confession, chapter 25.6, named the pope the Antichrist. Many modern Presbyterian churches have since revised that line.
Luther, Calvin, Knox and the translators of the Geneva Bible notes all held forms of this view.

Historicist Protestants still defend the view in some circles. Roman Catholic writers reject it as polemic and note that it arose amid bitter conflict. Most modern evangelical scholars, futurist or not, have set it aside as reading later history into the text.
Does a papal title such as "Vicarius Filii Dei" really add up to 666?
The Latin letters can be made to total 666, but the title is not an official papal title, and the method could fit thousands of names.

The phrase means "Vicar (substitute) of the Son of God". Counting only the letters that are Roman numerals gives V5 + I1 + C100 + I1 + V5 + I1 + L50 + I1 + I1 + D500 + I1 = 666. The phrase appears in the forged Donation of Constantine, but it has not been a formal title of the popes. Their usual title is "Vicar of Christ". The method also selects which letters to count and ignores the rest. The fulfilled reading adds a deeper point. John told his first readers to calculate the number of a man in their own time (Revelation 13:18; 1:3). A medieval or modern office could not be the answer they needed.
Worked sum: VICARIVS FILII DEI gives V(5) I(1) C(100) I(1) V(5) I(1) L(50) I(1) I(1) D(500) I(1) = 666.
The Donation of Constantine was shown to be a forgery by Lorenzo Valla in 1440.

Some Seventh-day Adventist and historicist writers have long cited this title as the solution. Many in those traditions now treat it with caution. Catholic writers point out that it was never an official papal title.
What did Irenaeus say about the name "Lateinos" and 666?
Irenaeus (around AD 180) offered "Lateinos" (Latin man) as a possible answer since "the Latins now rule". He did not apply it to a church leader, and he urged caution.

In Against Heresies 5.30.3 Irenaeus discusses several names that total 666 in Greek, including Euanthas, Lateinos and Teitan. Lateinos counts as L30 + A1 + T300 + E5 + I10 + N50 + O70 + S200 = 666. He thought it "very probable" because the Latins, that is, the Romans, ruled the world. Later Protestants used this to point at the Latin church, but that was not Irenaeus's meaning. He also refused to be certain, saying that if the name were meant to be known now, John would have said it. On the fulfilled reading, Irenaeus's link to Roman rule fits well: the beast was the Roman power of John's day. Irenaeus also knew manuscripts reading 616 (5.30.1).
Irenaeus wrote about AD 180, about a century after Revelation, and already had several proposals to weigh.

Futurists note that Irenaeus expected a future Antichrist and dated Revelation late in Domitian's reign (5.30.3). They use him as an early witness against a Neronic solution. Preterists reply that his phrase about the vision being seen "towards the end of Domitian's reign" is open to debate.
What does it show that even Martin Luther and Napoleon were "proved" to be 666?
It shows that the method works for enemies on every side. When the same tool can tag both a pope and the reformer who opposed him, it proves nothing.

During the Reformation, Catholic polemicists turned the number on Martin Luther. Using a coded alphabet (A to I as 1 to 9, K to S as 10 to 90, T to Z as 100 to 700), "MARTIN LUTERA" was made to total 666. Meanwhile, Protestant writers counted popes and papal titles. In the early 1800s, many British writers named Napoleon. Hester Thrale Piozzi recorded that village women in Wales had found that his titles in Roman numerals came to 666. Each side found the answer it wanted. The fulfilled reading draws a plain lesson: the method serves the interpreter's fears, not the text. Scripture's own time markers and Old Testament background must guide us.
Worked sum for MARTIN LUTERA in that alphabet: M30 + A1 + R80 + T100 + I9 + N40 + L20 + U200 + T100 + E5 + R80 + A1 = 666.
Napoleon was also called "Apollyon" (Revelation 9:11) by some who claimed his Corsican name meant "destroyer".

Historicist writers have argued that some of these identifications held real insight into the spirit of tyranny. Futurists agree the past guesses failed, but they say this only shows the beast has not yet come, not that the search is wrong.
How were Hitler and Mussolini fitted to 666, and what does that teach?
By invented rules: Hitler with A=100, Mussolini with the Roman numerals of "VV IL DUCE". Both were real tyrants, but neither was the beast John described.

Hitler persecuted and numbered the Jewish people, so many in the 1930s and 1940s named him. Yet the numbers tattooed in camps were serial numbers, not 666. To fit his name, one counter began the alphabet at A=100: H107 + I108 + T119 + L111 + E104 + R117 = 666. Why not A=1, as Hebrew and Greek counting do? Mussolini's slogan "VV IL DUCE" ("long live the leader") gives V5 + V5 + I1 + L50 + D500 + V5 + C100 = 666. A 1940 booklet claimed he fulfilled forty-nine prophecies of Antichrist. One later writer even suggested Hitler might return from the dead as the beast. The fulfilled reading honours the real evil of these men but notes that Revelation's beast was "near" for John's readers (1:3).

Many teachers of every school say tyrants like Hitler show the "spirit of antichrist" (1 John 4:3) at work in history. Some futurists argue that such figures foreshadow a final, greater ruler still to come.
What do the claims about Kissinger, Sadat, Reagan, Gorbachev and Clinton teach us?
They show "adjustment theology": a person is the Antichrist until events prove otherwise, then the label moves to the next leader. None of these claims came true.

In recent decades, many leaders have been named. Henry Kissinger was a "man of peace". Anwar Sadat was named. Ronald Wilson Reagan had six letters in each name, and his California home was at 666 St Cloud Road (the number was later changed to 668). After the 1981 shooting, some linked James Brady's head wound to Revelation 13:3. Mikhail Gorbachev's 1992 welcome in Israel was read as an Antichrist covenant sign. A 1993 Time cover was said to give Bill Clinton "horns". Each claim was later quietly dropped. Jesus warned against being led astray by those who say "the time is near" (Luke 21:8). The fulfilled reading asks why we should trust new guesses when every past guess failed.
Reagan: "Ronald (6) Wilson (6) Reagan (6)" letters, which is three sixes, not 666.
Gorbachev was welcomed at Ben-Gurion airport in June 1992, and some books named him the Antichrist.

Responsible futurist scholars also reject naming living people. They warn against date-setting while still holding that a final Antichrist will come. Many say speculation by popular writers does not discredit the doctrine itself.
Can the beast be someone who lived long after John, such as a future or revived ruler?
On the fulfilled reading, no. Revelation says its events were "near", so the beast had to be someone the first readers could know.

Some writers set Nero aside because they date Revelation to about AD 95, long after Nero died in AD 68. One such writer suggested that Hitler might be raised from the dead as the beast, since the beast had a "fatal wound" that was healed (Revelation 13:3). The fulfilled reading objects that this approach skips the book's time texts. Revelation opens and closes by saying its events must "shortly take place" and "the time is near" (1:1, 3; 22:6, 10). One writer quoted Revelation 1:1 and 1:3 but left out the words "shortly" and "near". The beast must fit a first-century audience. Leaping two thousand years ahead to find him ignores what John told his readers.
Revelation 22:10: "Don't seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is at hand" (WEB). Compare Daniel 8:26, where a vision is sealed because it is far off.
Nero died on 9 June AD 68 by his own hand with a sword (Suetonius, Nero 49).

Futurists read "shortly" (en tachei) as "quickly once it begins" or as God's view of time (2 Peter 3:8). Those who hold a late date (about AD 95) cite Irenaeus. Some see Nero as a type of a future ruler, linked to the "Nero redivivus" legend behind Revelation 17:11.
Is "666" the same as three sixes in a row?
No. Revelation gives one number, "six hundred sixty-six". Three separate sixes, as in Reagan's letter count or a "66th" item, are a different thing.

Revelation 13:18 says the number is "six hundred sixty-six". In many Greek manuscripts it is written in words, and in others with three Greek numeral letters, chi (600), xi (60) and stigma (6). It is a single sum, not a pattern of three digits. Many modern claims miss this. Three six-letter names, three bars said to be sixes, or "www" read as three Hebrew vavs all give 6-6-6, not 666. When Time named Bill Clinton its 66th "Man of the Year", a caller saw a link, though the number was 600 short. The fulfilled reading uses this as a simple test: a solution that does not give the sum 666 has not even met the text's terms.
Greek numerals: χ (600) + ξ (60) + ϛ (6) = 666. This is one number.
Three Hebrew vavs (each 6) total 18 if added, not 666.

Scholars of all schools agree that 666 is a single number. Some idealists see symbolism in the repeated six, a triple falling short of God's seven. Even they treat the number as a whole, not as three digits.
Is 666 already hidden in credit cards and the banking system?
No. Claims that cards carry a 666 prefix were false. Such fears resemble superstition more than Bible study.

In the early 1980s one writer claimed that the "666 system" was already in place, with a 666 prefix on Visa and MasterCard numbers and on government documents. The claims did not hold. Card numbers follow issuer codes, and 666 is not a standard prefix. A short story about a time traveller who gives Isaac Newton a calculator shows how superstition works. The traveller divides 81,918 by 123, the screen glows 666, and Newton attacks him as a servant of Satan. The fulfilled reading warns that fear of a number, apart from its biblical meaning, makes Christians like that frightened figure. Revelation calls for wisdom (13:18), not dread of digits.
Worked check: 123 x 666 = 81,918, a random sum that means nothing.
The predictions of the early 1980s that a 666 money system was days away did not come true.

Some futurist writers still expect a future electronic economy to be used for control. More careful futurists, like Thomas Ice and Timothy Demy, admit that the Bible does not mention credit cards or computers. They treat technology as making fulfilment possible, not as a fulfilment already present.
What did "let him who has understanding calculate the number" mean for the first readers?
It invited them to work out a name they could know. On the fulfilled reading, the beast lived then, so today he is not alive but buried.

John writes: "Here is wisdom. He who has understanding, let him calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man" (13:18). The call is to the readers of the seven churches, who were promised a blessing for hearing and keeping the prophecy (1:3). A riddle they could not solve would give no wisdom and no blessing. They lived under Roman rule and faced persecution. They knew the names of their rulers and could count letters as people then often did. Graffiti at Pompeii, buried in AD 79, reads "I love her whose number is 545". On the fulfilled reading, the answer lay in their own history. The beast is not alive somewhere today; he belongs to the first century.
A Pompeii wall inscription: "I love her whose number is 545", a name hidden as a number.
Revelation 1:3: a blessing on those who read, hear and keep what is written, "for the time is at hand" (WEB).

Futurists say the "understanding" will be given to believers in the last generation when the beast appears, as Daniel's words were sealed until the end (Daniel 12:4, 9). Idealists take 666 as a symbol of humanity in rebellion, so that every age must discern it.
